definition: Chronic psychosis refers to psychosis in a long-standing or later stage form rather than an early-stage episode. In the source, it is discussed as a persistent stage of psychosis in which difficulties such as impaired theory of mind and poor functioning may continue beyond general neurocognitive problems.

reasons: The packet does not define “chronic psychosis” as a long-standing or later-stage form rather than an early-stage episode; it only mentions “chronic patients” in passing.

The packet supports discussion of theory of mind (ToM) deficits and their relation to functioning in chronic patients, but it does not substantiate the definition’s broader framing about “persistent stage of psychosis” continuing beyond “general neurocognitive problems.”

The definition includes elements (“impaired theory of mind and poor functioning may continue beyond general neurocognitive problems”) that are only partially supported: the packet discusses ToM deficits not being fully accounted for by general neurocognitive deficits and ToM impairment affecting functioning, but it does not support the claim that this “continues beyond” neurocognitive problems as stated.
The packet does not define chronic psychosis as a long-standing or later-stage form of psychosis, so that sense is unsupported.

The statement that this is a persistent stage in which impaired theory of mind and poor functioning continue beyond general neurocognitive problems overstates the source; the article only says these deficits and their effects are noted in chronic patients and are not fully accounted for by other neurocognitive deficits.
